text:
A pace plan treats the body as an engine with a fixed output, but the body also runs on a limited fuel supply. A trained runner stores roughly 400 to 500 grams of glycogen in the muscles and liver, which is about 2,000 calories. Marathon pace burns close to 100 calories per mile, so that supply runs out somewhere near mile 20.

After that, the body has to rely on fat oxidation, which produces ATP more slowly. Consider a runner who ran a cool, flat first half fast to gain some early seconds. At mile 12, those splits looked sustainable. Now the fuel system can't release enough energy to hold them, and the runner has spent more than the body had to give.

Other factors widen the gap: heat, dehydration that costs two percent of body mass, and eccentric damage to the quads. Then the runner hits the wall.

To prevent this, run negative splits with discipline, take in 60 to 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour, and do long runs that train your body to burn fat before race day.
